title: Pronominal suffixes on nouns

objectives.can: Identify the pronominal suffix on a noun: its person, gender and number.

explanation.summary: Hebrew says 'my father', 'his wife', 'your house' by fastening a short pronoun to the end of the noun. These suffixes are everywhere in the Bible, and each one tells you the person, gender and number of the owner.

sections.heading: A pronoun on the end of the noun
body: English puts a separate word before the noun: 'my', 'his', 'your'. Hebrew writes the owner on the end of the noun itself: אָבִי is 'my father', אָבִיו is 'his father', אָבִיךָ is 'your father'. The suffix is part of the written word. In the word-by-word display it is the feature Suffix, shown as a code.

A code such as 3ms reads: person 3, gender m (masculine), number s (singular): 'his'. 1cs is 'my', where c stands for 'common', the one form for both genders. 2fs is 'your' to a woman, 3mp is 'their' of men, and 1cp is 'our'. The suffix describes the owner. The noun has its own gender and number, and they are marked as usual.

sections.heading: The nine suffixes
body: The forms below are those regularly met on nouns. There are two sets, one for singular nouns and one for plural nouns, and in the plural set most forms have a י. Several suffixes have more than one form, depending on the final sound of the noun.
The table gives the endings in a short, plain way, written with a hyphen. They are not words to look up; learn to recognise them at the end of a word.

sections.heading: Singular and plural noun
body: The set tells you the number of the noun, not of the owner. בְּנוֹ is 'his son', one son, and בָּנָיו is 'his sons', several sons; in both the owner is 'he'. In the same way דְּבָרוֹ is 'his word' and דְּבָרָיו is 'his words'. When you meet a suffix, ask two questions: who owns it, and is the noun one or many?

The suffix is attached to a shortened form of the noun, much like the construct state: בַּיִת, 'house', gives בֵּיתוֹ, 'his house', and דָּבָר gives דְּבָרוֹ. The noun may shift its vowels, so look at the end of the word first.

sections.heading: A noun with a suffix is definite
body: A noun with a suffix is definite: 'my father' means a particular father, so it cannot also take the article. In a construct chain the suffix on the last noun makes the whole chain definite: בֵּית אָבִיךָ is 'your father's house'. The first noun is in the construct state, and the second has the suffix.
Prefixed particles still go on the front of such a word: בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ is 'to his wife', with the prefix ב and the suffix 3ms.

misunderstandings: The י in -ָיו or -ֶיךָ does not mean that the owner is plural. It marks a plural noun. The owner is in the code: 3ms is one man in both אָבִיו and אֲבֹתָיו.
The noun itself may change when a suffix is added: אִשָּׁה becomes אִשְׁתּוֹ. Find the suffix at the end of the word first, then recognise the shortened noun before it.
The letter c in 1cs and 1cp means 'common', not a count: the first person has one form for men and women.
3ms and 3mp, or 2ms and 2mp, are different suffixes. The m shows the gender and the last letter shows the number, so 3mp is 'their' and not 'his'.

deeper.heading: The same suffixes elsewhere
body: The same pronoun endings turn up on prepositions (לוֹ, 'to him'), on the object marker (אֹתוֹ) and, in a different form, on verbs. Once you can recognise them on nouns you have most of what you need for those later lessons. Some of the shapes differ slightly, so each is taught where it occurs.
